body.text: That drive has not yet reached commercial-scale metallisation in Australia. Metallisation remains a particularly challenging bottleneck in the critical minerals and rare earths supply chain. Rare earth elements such as neodymium have to undergo metallisation to be transformed into high-purity metals that can be used as raw materials for high-tech components, defence systems and green energy technology. The International Energy Agency (IEA) identifies metallisation and magnet manufacturing as among the most constrained stages of the rare earths supply chain. Refining, the step before metallisation, is also concentrated. In 2024, China accounted for 91% of global refined output of magnet rare earths. The IEA reports that the market for magnet rare earths is worth less than US$10 billion a year, but estimates that a disruption to supply could have an economic impact of US$6.5 trillion annually. This reflects how much economic security depends on these supply chains.

Australia is investing in the step before metallisation. luka’s Eneabba refinery in Western Australia, supported by a $1.65 billion loan through the Critical Minerals Facility, will produce rare earth oxides. This is still short of metallisation. Refining is highly capital-intensive and metallisation is technically complex, with very few operators outside China. Despite the challenges, Australia has some advantages to offer.

For one, the energy-intensive process of metallisation requires large amounts of reliable, low-emissions power. Australia’s renewable energy resources could give it a natural edge here. Researchers at Monash and UNSW argue that the answer for Australia’s green export industries is precincts where processors share power, water and ports, and their modelling of a proposed South Australian green iron hub found that integration can cut power costs by 20–30% compared with standalone projects. The same logic could apply to metallisation wherein sharing infrastructure means each plant does not have to build its own electricity system. For example, Gladstone, which hosts heavy industry on shared infrastructure and sits next to planned renewable energy zones, is one plausible site for a metallisation precinct.

Through bilateral and minilateral frameworks like the Quad, Australia should also secure financing for metallisation projects. Australia and the United States have ramped up efforts to unlock investment in critical mineral projects across Australia. In October 2025, the United States’ export credit agency, EXIM, issued letters of interest worth more than US$2.2 billion for seven Australian critical minerals projects. Canberra should push for metallisation to feature in the next round. Such financing agreements can also be paired with offtake agreements, as Japanese backers did with Lynas, so buyers can commit to the output. Domestically, mechanisms like the Critical Minerals Production Tax Incentive provide an offset on processing costs, but do not cover the cost of constructing a plant. Similarly, the Critical Minerals Facility backs commercially ready projects, which may create a catch-22 for metallisation projects. Domestic policy should therefore direct capital support to metallisation specifically, while using international financing partnerships to complement it.

Industry groups have also argued that lengthy environmental approval timelines can cause severe gridlocks. With the environmental reform laws passed last year, the government aims to speed up decisions for priority projects like critical minerals. But to further address this, federal departments such as the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW) and the Department of Industry, Science and Resources (DISR) should collaborate to streamline project approvals specifically for midstream metallisation hubs. Instead of project-by-project approvals, government departments can assess precinct-level approvals.

The push towards critical minerals supply chain resilience was born in response to China’s dominance of rare earth refining and the stages that follow. A robust and credible de-risking agenda must include concrete steps towards building domestic midstream processing. For Australia, moving up the value chain is not just an industrial objective, but also a geostrategic one. By partnering with international allies to overcome capital and domestic constraints, Australia can anchor supply chain security and provide economic security to its partners in the Indo-Pacific.
